headline: Recommended City Council rules on when street event barriers are required, who pays for them, and a hardship fund, passed unanimously.
summary: A report on Flock cameras and license plate readers will recommend no added local limits. The City Solicitor will research local options for tobacco and vape sales. Police reported 77 calls for service, including 50 directed patrols, in the Capitol Commons garage area from September 14 through November 2, 2026.
decisions: Approved the October 2026 meeting minutes, passed unanimously.
Recommended that the City Council set rules for when vehicle barriers are required, who pays for them, and a funding mechanism for hardship cases, passed unanimously.
Approved preparing a report to City Council recommending no added local restrictions on Flock cameras and license plate readers, passed unanimously.
Approved a request for more legal research and recommendations from the City Solicitor on tobacco and vape product sales, with no opposing votes recorded.

decision_titles: Vehicle barrier rules and funding for street events
Flock cameras and automated license plate readers
Legal research on tobacco and vape product sales
plain_text:
C I T Y  O F  C O N C O R D
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
141 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Public Safety Advisory Board
Thursday, November 19, 2026 (3:00 p.m.) – City Council Chambers
DRAFT Meeting Minutes
Members Present:  Lisa Brown, Bouzned (Moe) Djabelarbi, Steve Edwards, Jessica Eskeland, 
Councilor Jeff Foote, Councilor and Chair Amanda Grady Sexton, Natch Greys, Councilor 
Jennifer Kretovic, Councilor Ali Sekou
City Staff:  Deputy Police Chief Matt Casey, Fire Chief John Chisholm, City Solicitor John 
Conforti, Deputy Fire Chief Mick Costello, Police Chief Barrett Moulton, Acting Deputy Police 
Chief Patrick Ofrias
Minute Taker: Amanda Grady Sexton
Chair Grady Sexton called the meeting to order at 3:00 p.m.
Approval of October 2026 Meeting Minutes
Jessica Eskeland moved to approve the October 2026 meeting minutes. Natch Greys seconded 
the motion. There was no discussion or proposed amendment. The motion passed unanimously.
Drug Enforcement Administration Presentation
The scheduled representative of the Drug Enforcement Administration was unable to attend the 
meeting. The presentation will be rescheduled for a future meeting.
Traffic Barrier Deployment and Funding
At the previous PSAB meeting, Deputy Fire Chief Costello reviewed the vehicle barrier system 
purchased through a Homeland Security grant. The system is deployed at certain street events 
to protect attendees from vehicles entering closed areas. Staff explained that deployment, 
removal, staffing, and maintaining emergency access require substantial labor, at a cost of 
approximately $1,500 per deployment. General Services deploys the equipment, and first 
responders must remain available to open the barriers for emergency vehicles.
Staff identified Market Days, Halloween Howl, Midnight Merriment, and the annual Holiday Tree 
Lighting as City-sponsored events for which the City covers the cost of barrier deployment. The 
Board was asked to consider which non-City-sponsored events require barriers and how to fund 
their use when an event organizer demonstrates financial hardship.
Members discussed whether all events involving major street closures should require barriers or
whether the permitting process should rely on an assessment by the Police Department, Fire 
Department, and Code Administration. Members noted that risks include intentional attacks, 
impaired drivers, and drivers who are confused or experiencing another emergency. Appropriate
barrier placement may vary for parades, road races, events with a central gathering area, and 
events extending along a route. Members also discussed the need to consider events elsewhere
in the City, including Loudon Road and Penacook.
Several members supported allowing the Police Department, Fire Department, and Code 
Administration to determine when barriers are required through the existing event review 
process. Discussion also addressed consistency between City-sponsored and other events and 
potential municipal liability when barriers are available but not used.
C I T Y  O F  C O N C O R D
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
241 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
During its November meeting, City Solicitor John Conforti reviewed the legal and liability 
considerations associated with the City’s newly acquired vehicle barrier system. He emphasized
that the decision to require the system at any event must be based solely on public safety 
needs, not on an event sponsor’s financial resources or ability to pay.
The Board reviewed two potential funding approaches: City funding for all non-City-sponsored 
events, or payment by event organizers with a hardship funding option. The estimated 
deployment expense discussed was approximately $1,500 per event. 
Police representatives provided additional information about the current event review process 
involving the Police Department, Fire Department, and Code Administration. They explained 
that up to 20 special events with road closures were identified citywide in the prior year, 
although not all would necessarily require the enhanced barriers. The discussion included 
downtown events, parades, and road races in other neighborhoods. The deployment charge 
generally reflects installation and removal rather than the number of days barriers remain in 
place.
Natch Greys moved to recommend that the City Council: (1) authorize the Concord Fire 
Department, Concord Police Department, and Code Administration to determine when vehicle 
barriers are required through the existing event permitting process; (2) require sponsoring 
organizations and event organizers to pay the costs associated with barrier deployment; (3) 
establish eligibility criteria for organizations demonstrating financial hardship; and (4) direct the 
City Manager to establish a funding mechanism to assist event permit applicants who 
demonstrate financial hardship, ensuring that required barriers are deployed at all events where 
they are deemed necessary, regardless of an organizer’s ability to pay.
Jessica Eskeland seconded the motion. The motion passed unanimously.
Flock Cameras and Automated License Plate Readers
The Board reviewed a City Council referral concerning Flock cameras and automated license 
plate readers. City Solicitor Conforti summarized New Hampshire’s restrictive statutory 
framework, including RSA 261:75-b and RSA 236:130. He reported that the previously 
anticipated sunset of the license plate reader restrictions had been removed and that the 
restrictions remain in effect.
Discussion addressed limitations on law enforcement acquisition and use, permitted purposes, 
data retention and verification requirements, as well as concerns about private databases, 
surveillance and emerging artificial intelligence capabilities. Members also discussed potential 
narrowly tailored municipal uses of imaging technology in other contexts, with appropriate limits 
on data collection and use. No purchase or deployment of Flock cameras was proposed.
Members agreed that the existing state statutory framework provides substantial restrictions and
that further local restrictions were not warranted at this time. Jessica Eskeland made a motion to
prepare a report to City Council summarizing the discussion and recommending no additional 
local restrictions. The motion was seconded by Councilor Foote and was passed unanimously.
Tobacco and Vape Product Sales
The Board considered a referral from a Ward 9 resident expressing concern about combustible 
tobacco products, the proliferation of vape shops, and possible sales to individuals under age 
21. City Solicitor Conforti discussed the existing state regulatory framework, including RSA 126-
K, and the limits of municipal authority. He requested additional time to research legally

341 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
available local options to present to the Board, including measures that could reinforce 
enforcement or increase public awareness.
Members expressed interest in addressing the resident’s concerns through a possible 
ordinance, resolution, or proclamation. Discussion included a proposal under consideration in 
Manchester. Police representatives explained that the New Hampshire Liquor Commission 
oversees tobacco and vape product enforcement and described concerns involving some vape 
cartridges containing cannabis-related substances. Fire safety concerns associated with 
rechargeable batteries from vape cartridges were also discussed.
Natch Greys moved to request additional legal research and recommendations from the City 
Solicitor. Lisa Brown seconded the motion. No opposing votes were recorded. The Board 
agreed to revisit the topic at its January 21, 2027, meeting.
Department and Community Updates
The Board congratulated the newly appointed Police Chief. Natch Greys thanked the Police 
Department for its response to an election-day concern involving a tent set up in an 
impermissible location near a polling place.
Downtown Safety and Homelessness
Members discussed reports of uncomfortable and concerning encounters downtown, including a
reported incident near Eagle Square and ongoing concerns about the Storrs Street area. Police 
representatives described ongoing foot patrols, contacts with business owners, responses to 
aggressive behavior, and the challenges of enforcement in public spaces. They emphasized that
reports involving threatening or aggressive conduct are taken seriously and investigated when 
warranted.
Police staff reported that a review of downtown activity did not show an overall increase in 
reported crime. Simple assaults were lower in the reviewed 2026 period, and most involved 
known parties or existing disputes. Police also reported 77 calls for service, including 50 
directed patrols, in the Capitol Commons garage area from September 14 through November 2, 
2026. The Department explained that changes in how homelessness-related calls are 
categorized can affect comparisons across years. The Fire Department described its own 
system for identifying calls associated with homelessness and distinguishing direct from 
incidental involvement.
Members emphasized the distinction between homelessness and criminal or threatening 
conduct and discussed the importance of both actual safety and the public’s perception of 
safety. The Board also discussed seasonal changes in the downtown population, the opening of 
winter shelter services, and concerns about public spaces and nightlife establishments. Police 
representatives stated that they work with liquor enforcement when recurring problems involving
licensed establishments arise and reported no particular emerging pattern at the establishment 
discussed.
The City Solicitor explained that a recent challenge concerning loitering is directed at the state 
statute rather than specifically at the City of Concord. Staff discussed the City’s efforts to enforce
laws while respecting constitutional rights and safeguarding personal property. A member 
suggested examining practices in other communities, including Portland, Maine, and 
Manchester. Staff indicated they could explore approaches being used elsewhere.
C I T Y  O F  C O N C O R D
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
441 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Future Agenda Items and Meeting Schedule
The Board agreed not to hold its regular December meeting unless a new referral or other 
urgent matter requires consideration. The next regular meeting is scheduled for Thursday, 
January 21, 2027, at 3:00 p.m. The tobacco sales referral will return for discussion at that 
meeting. The DEA presentation will be rescheduled when feasible. Downtown safety and 
homelessness may be revisited at a future meeting.
Adjournment
Lisa Brown moved to adjourn the meeting at 4:35 p.m. Jessica Eskeland seconded the motion. 
The motion passed unanimously.
